screens.title: Streaming Telemetry with gRPC and NETCONF/YANG
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we shift from periodic polling to continuous, model-driven telemetry. You will learn why SNMP polling struggles with modern, dynamic networks, and how streaming telemetry provides near real-time, high-granularity operational data. We'll cover the role of YANG as the schema language that gives telemetry structure, and compare two transport approaches: NETCONF, the established XML-over-SSH protocol, and gRPC with Protocol Buffers, a high-performance streaming transport often used on Cisco IOS XE. I will walk you through the essential IOS XE steps to enable gRPC, create a telemetry subscription that uses YANG XPath filters, and the conceptual options for a collector implemented in Python. Along the way we'll pinpoint common mistakes — like incorrect YANG paths or firewall blocks — and practical checks to verify the stream is active. This chapter matters because modern automation, analytics, and closed-loop operations all depend on reliable, timely data. By the end, you'll understand what data to ask for, how it's encoded, and the network-side configuration to start streaming interface statistics to a collector.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.5 › Streaming Telemetry
Streaming Telemetry with gRPC and NETCONF/YANG
From push-based streams to YANG-defined schemas and transport options for IOS XE.
In this lesson

Understand why polling can miss transient events and how push-based telemetry delivers higher granularity and lower latency, how YANG structures telemetry, and how NETCONF and gRPC differ as transports.

Coming up

IOS XE configuration snippets, a conceptual Python collector discussion, verification commands, and common mistakes to avoid during deployment.

Key Takeaway

Streaming telemetry uses YANG schemas and efficient transports like gRPC to provide scalable, near real-time operational data that polling cannot reliably deliver at high granularity.

Concept Map
SNMP vs Streaming → YANG → Transport (NETCONF/gRPC)
Visual: cards show push-based streams, YANG blueprint, and gRPC wire efficiency.
Explore Key Topics
Polling limits
Why SNMP snapshots miss transient spikes and add latency.
YANG models
Model-driven, vendor-neutral data structure for telemetry.
gRPC transport
Efficient binary encoding and streaming patterns with Protobuf.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives will frame our exploration. First, you will explain the limitations of polling systems like SNMP and why they fall short for high-granularity, real-time observability. For example, you should be able to describe how a five-minute poll can miss a one-second performance spike and why that matters for troubleshooting. Second, you will describe how YANG models structure both configuration and operational state data, enabling consistent parsing and programmatic consumption across vendors. Practice reading a simple YANG path as an XPath-like selector and see how that reduces ambiguity. Third, you will understand the difference between NETCONF and gRPC as telemetry transports: NETCONF provides transaction-backed XML over SSH, while gRPC with Protocol Buffers offers efficient binary serialization and streaming. Finally, you will be able to configure basic streaming telemetry on Cisco IOS XE: enable gRPC, define a subscription with encoding and an XPath filter, and point the device to a collector. Each objective ties to practical checks you can run on a router, such as showing telemetry subscriptions and verifying collector connectivity. This focus helps you move from concept to repeatable practice.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Outcomes
screens.narratorSegment: In addition to conceptual knowledge, you will practice concrete validation steps. You'll learn to verify gRPC status and subscription state on IOS XE using commands that show whether the device is connected to the collector and the last-sent time. You will interpret what Disconnected, Connecting, and Active states mean in practice and how to proceed — for instance, checking the collector's firewall and service availability. You'll also learn how to reason about resource impact: streaming at sub-second intervals improves visibility but increases C P U and bandwidth usage, and you'll be able to explain tradeoffs and monitoring strategies. Finally, you'll become familiar with common troubleshooting checks: validating YANG XPath filters, ensuring collector redundancy, and confirming that buffer limits are handled or mitigated. These practical skills turn understanding into operational competence: you can both configure and verify a telemetry pipeline and decide when a push model is the right fit.

screens.title: Why SNMP polling falls short for modern networks
screens.narratorSegment: Start by defining the problem: traditional SNMP is pull-based. A network management system periodically queries devices for counter values or state. That approach works for coarse, infrequent monitoring, but it creates observable gaps. If you poll every five minutes, a one-second performance spike can occur and disappear between polls, leaving no trace. Polling also scales poorly: trying to poll many devices every second creates enormous overhead and increases latency. Streaming telemetry addresses this by letting devices push data either on change or at high frequencies, so you capture transient events and reduce the need for constant polling requests. A concrete example: collecting interface counters every second from hundreds of devices via polling would flood the NMS and consume C P U on both ends. With streaming telemetry, devices send updates only when configured or when a change occurs, lowering management-plane overhead and improving timeliness. A common misconception is that push always means more bandwidth; while higher-frequency streaming does increase data volume, well-designed subscriptions and YANG filters let you limit what you stream. The practical takeaway: choose streaming when you need sub-second visibility and use filters to control load.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.5 › Polling vs Streaming
SNMP Polling (Pull)
  • Periodic requests from the NMS.
  • May miss transient, sub-poll events.
  • Scale issues at high poll rates.
Example: 5-minute polling interval misses a 10-second outage.
Streaming Telemetry (Push)
  • Device pushes updates by event or frequency.
  • Near real-time visibility for transient events.
  • Use YANG filters to limit data to what matters.
Example: streaming interface counters at 1s intervals captures bursts and short spikes.
Concrete Scenario

Imagine troubleshooting packet drops that last 200 milliseconds. With a five-minute polling window, you will not see them. Streaming telemetry configured for sub-second or one-second updates records those bursts and lets analytics correlate them with events.

Key Takeaway

Use streaming when you need accurate, high-granularity observability. Use filters to manage resource use.

Check Your Understanding
If you need to capture sub-second transient events across many interfaces, is SNMP polling at 5 minutes adequate? Why or why not?

screens.title: What is Streaming Telemetry?
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define streaming telemetry precisely. Streaming telemetry is a model where devices push structured operational data to a collector either when values change or at a configured frequency. It differs from logs and polling because data is delivered proactively and typically in a structured, schema-driven format. The advantage is immediate availability: collectors see changes soon after they occur, enabling faster anomaly detection and closed-loop automation. Concretely, you can stream interface statistics at one-second intervals so analytics detect link flaps or microbursts that would be invisible to coarse polling. A useful mental model is that telemetry turns devices into observability publishers and the collector into a subscriber that ingests time-series updates. A common misconception is that streaming always produces massive volumes; the reality is that using YANG filters and sensible update policies (on-change, periodic with tuned intervals) lets you control volume while still gaining timely data. The takeaway is clear: streaming telemetry trades configuration complexity for timeliness and granularity, and when combined with YANG it becomes machine-friendly for automation. What is Streaming Telemetry? means devices push structured operational data on change or periodically; yang filters and update policies control the volume and content.. In practical terms, a push-based, event-driven approach to operational data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.5 › Streaming Telemetry
Definition

Streaming telemetry is a push-based method where devices proactively send structured operational data to a collector on change or at configured intervals. It is model-driven using YANG.

Key properties
  • Push-based delivery for near real-time visibility.
  • YANG-modeled payloads for consistent parsing.
  • Supports on-change and periodic update policies.
Analogy

Think of streaming telemetry as subscribing to a data feed for each device. Instead of asking for a weather snapshot every hour, you get a live feed of temperature updates when they change.

Key Takeaway

Streaming telemetry provides timely, structured updates that support automation and analytics when paired with YANG models and proper update policies.

Concrete example

Stream interface statistics at 1 second intervals to capture microbursts and short-lived packet drops, then feed those series into analytics for anomaly detection.

screens.title: YANG Data Models: the schema for telemetry
screens.narratorSegment: YANG is central to model-driven telemetry. It defines the shape and semantics of configuration and operational state so both devices and collectors agree on what each field means. In practice, YANG modules describe configuration nodes like interface IP addresses and operational nodes like interface statistics or C P U utilization. They can also define RPC operations and notification formats. When you specify a YANG XPath filter in a telemetry subscription, you're asking the device to stream a particular subtree defined by the model. A concrete example: the path /interfaces-state/interface/statistics points to per-interface counters described in the YANG module for interfaces. A common misconception is that YANG is a transport; it is not. YANG only defines structure and semantics; NETCONF or gRPC carry the data. Because YANG is vendor-neutral, collectors can parse telemetry from different devices consistently, simplifying automation and analytics. The practical skill is reading a YANG path and matching it to the telemetry you need, which reduces trial-and-error and avoids empty subscriptions. YANG Data Models: the schema for telemetry means yang defines what telemetry contains; transports move it. use yang paths to precisely specify telemetry data.. In practical terms, how yang defines configuration, operational state, rpcs, and notifications. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.5 › YANG Models
YANG roles
  • Define configuration schema (what can be set).
  • Define operational state (what is reported).
  • Define RPCs and notification structures.
Concrete example
A subscription with XPath /interfaces-state/interface/statistics targets per-interface counters described by the interfaces YANG model. If the path is incorrect, no data will be returned.
Why YANG matters

YANG gives a consistent, machine-readable blueprint. Collectors parse structured data rather than vendor-specific messages.

Key Takeaway

Use YANG paths to limit telemetry payloads to only the fields your analytics require.

screens.title: NETCONF and gRPC: how data gets moved
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding transports is about tradeoffs. NETCONF is an IETF protocol that uses XML encoding and typically runs over SSH. It is transaction-aware and well-suited to configuration tasks with strong operational semantics. NETCONF can also be used to retrieve state and subscribe to notifications, but XML encoding and SSH add overhead compared to binary transports. gRPC, by contrast, uses Protocol Buffers for serialization and HTTP/2 for transport; it supports streaming patterns, including bidirectional streams, and is generally more efficient on the wire. For streaming telemetry, gRPC's efficiency and native support for streaming make it attractive on IOS XE, especially when high-frequency updates are required. A common misconception is that NETCONF is obsolete; it remains useful for configuration transactions and for environments where XML and SSH are preferred. In practice, choose NETCONF for configuration and RPCs when you need transactional guarantees, and choose gRPC/Protobuf for high-performance telemetry streaming. Both depend on YANG models for the data structure; the transport only affects encoding and session behavior. NETCONF and gRPC: how data gets moved means netconf is xml-over-ssh and transaction-focused; grpc with protobuf is binary, http/2-based, and optimized for streaming high-frequency telemetry.. In practical terms, xml-over-ssh transaction model vs protobuf/http2 streaming. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.5 › Transports
NETCONF
  • XML encoding over SSH.
  • Transaction semantics for configuration.
  • Supports operational retrieval and notifications.
Best when you need transactional config changes and established XML tooling.
gRPC + Protobuf
  • Binary Protobuf encoding, HTTP/2 transport.
  • Native streaming patterns and high efficiency.
  • Common choice for high-frequency telemetry on IOS XE.
Best when you need efficient, streaming transport for high-granularity telemetry.
Decision rule

Use NETCONF for configuration and when XML/SSH is required. Use gRPC when you need efficient streaming telemetry and Protobuf serialization.

screens.title: Enable gRPC on Cisco IOS XE
screens.narratorSegment: Now we walk through the IOS XE configuration needed to enable gRPC so the device can act as a gRPC client or server depending on your model. Start in global configuration mode and enable the grpc service by specifying a port and ensuring the service is not shutdown. This step allows the device to establish or accept gRPC connections for telemetry. A concrete IOS snippet shows enabling gRPC on port 57000 and issuing no shutdown. After enabling gRPC you should verify the service state. A common trap is choosing a port already in use or forgetting firewall rules on the collector. Also confirm whether your deployment will use TLS; production setups should secure gRPC with TLS, whereas lab setups may use insecure channels for simplicity. The practical command and a quick verification step will prepare you to create subscriptions next. Remember: enabling gRPC is necessary but not sufficient — you still need to create telemetry subscriptions and ensure the collector is reachable. Enable gRPC on Cisco IOS XE means turn on the grpc service in global configuration, choose a port like 57000, and prepare for subscription configuration and collector connectivity checks.. In practical terms, minimal steps to open the grpc service for telemetry. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 9 › Chapter 9.5 › Enable gRPC
Command snippet
! Enable gRPC on the device
grpc
 port 57000

Ensure the chosen port is open on any intermediate firewalls and not used by other services.
Verification
show grpc
Confirm the service is enabled. In push models, the router often acts as the gRPC client and connects to the collector at the configured receiver address.
Safety note
Production use should secure gRPC with TLS and authentication. Lab setups may use insecure channels for testing, but never do that in production.

screens.title: Define a telemetry subscription on IOS XE
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson walks through creating a telemetry subscription on IOS XE. A subscription defines what to stream, how to encode it, the update policy, and the receiver details. Start by creating a named subscription. Choose an encoding such as the Key-Value Google Protocol Buffer encoding indicated by encode-kvgpb, set a YANG XPath filter to target the data subtree you need, select the stream mechanism like cisco-push, define update frequency using update-policy periodic with a millisecond interval, and finally provide the receiver's IP, port, and protocol. A concrete example: a subscription named MY_SUBSCRIPTION that encodes with encode-kvgpb, filters /interfaces-state/interface/statistics, uses stream cisco-push, updates every 1000 milliseconds, and points to a collector at 192.168.1.40:57000 via grpc-tcp. Common mistakes include typos in the XPath filter and forgetting that the receiver must be reachable and listening as a gRPC server. After you create the subscription, use show telemetry ietf subscription to confirm state and last-sent-time. Define a telemetry subscription on IOS XE means a subscription ties encoding, yang filter, update policy, stream, and receiver together to control what and how telemetry is sent.. In practical terms, create a subscription with encoding, filter, stream, update-policy, and receiver. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Example config
telemetry ietf subscription MY_SUBSCRIPTION
 encoding encode-kvgpb
 filter xpath /interfaces-state/interface/statistics
 stream cisco-push
 update-policy periodic 1000

Replace the receiver IP with your collector address and tune update-policy to manage load.
What each line does
  • encoding: serialization format for the payload.
  • filter xpath: YANG path selecting the subtree to stream.
  • stream: push mechanism used by IOS XE.
  • update-policy: periodic or on-change timing.
  • receiver: collector IP and transport protocol.
Verification command
show telemetry ietf subscription MY_SUBSCRIPTION
Look for State: Connected or Active and a Last-sent-time to confirm successful streaming.

screens.title: Consuming telemetry data: collector perspectives
screens.narratorSegment: Consuming streaming telemetry requires a collector that can accept, decode, and process data. The chapter explains an important nuance: when you configure the router with receiver ip address and protocol grpc-tcp, the router acts as a gRPC client and connects to the collector. That makes the collector a gRPC server in a push model. Building a full gRPC server in Python requires a. proto definition for the telemetry service and generated server stubs. Many practical deployments instead use a gNMI client for pull-mode telemetry or pre-built collector software. For CCIE-level understanding, know the conceptual flow: the router pushes Protobuf-encoded telemetry to the collector, which decodes based on YANG-derived Protobuf schemas and then stores or forwards the data. A common misconception is to implement a simple gRPC client when the router expects to be the client; you must implement a server or use tools that expose a gRPC endpoint. The safe approach in labs is to verify TCP connectivity with tcpdump and confirm SYNs from the router, then iterate toward a proper gRPC server or a gNMI-based pull client as your architecture requires.

screens.title: Common mistakes and safety notes
screens.narratorSegment: Deploying telemetry isn't only about commands; it's about avoiding common pitfalls. A frequent error is an incorrect YANG path: a small typo in an XPath filter leads to an empty stream. Always validate your YANG model and test filters with show telemetry commands. Network issues are another common blocker: firewalls often block gRPC ports like 57000, so verify connectivity using tcpdump or firewall logs. Collector availability matters; routers will buffer data up to a limit and then drop it if the collector is unreachable, so architect collector redundancy for critical metrics. Resource consumption is also a safety concern: highly granular streams increase C P U and bandwidth usage on devices — balance your need for granularity with device capabilities. Security must not be ignored: production deployments should use TLS and authentication for gRPC to prevent unauthorized access to telemetry. The practical habit is to start with conservative update policies and test one device before scaling, validate YANG paths, and build monitoring around collector health. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we shift from periodic polling to continuous, model-driven telemetry. You will learn why SNMP polling struggles with modern, dynamic networks, and how streaming telemetry provides near real-time, high-granularity operational data. We'll cover the role of YANG as the schema language that gives telemetry structure, and compare two transport approaches: NETCONF, the established XML-over-SSH protocol, and gRPC with Protocol Buffers, a high-performance streaming transport often used on Cisco IOS XE. I will walk you through the essential IOS XE steps to enable gRPC, create a telemetry subscription that uses YANG XPath filters, and the conceptual options for a collector implemented in Python. Along the way we'll pinpoint common mistakes — like incorrect YANG paths or firewall blocks — and practical checks to verify the stream is active. This chapter matters because modern automation, analytics, and closed-loop operations all depend on reliable, timely data. By the end, you'll understand what data to ask for, how it's encoded, and the network-side configuration to start streaming interface statistics to a collector.

These objectives will frame our exploration. First, you will explain the limitations of polling systems like SNMP and why they fall short for high-granularity, real-time observability. For example, you should be able to describe how a five-minute poll can miss a one-second performance spike and why that matters for troubleshooting. Second, you will describe how YANG models structure both configuration and operational state data, enabling consistent parsing and programmatic consumption across vendors. Practice reading a simple YANG path as an XPath-like selector and see how that reduces ambiguity. Third, you will understand the difference between NETCONF and gRPC as telemetry transports: NETCONF provides transaction-backed XML over SSH, while gRPC with Protocol Buffers offers efficient binary serialization and streaming. Finally, you will be able to configure basic streaming telemetry on Cisco IOS XE: enable gRPC, define a subscription with encoding and an XPath filter, and point the device to a collector. Each objective ties to practical checks you can run on a router, such as showing telemetry subscriptions and verifying collector connectivity. This focus helps you move from concept to repeatable practice.

In addition to conceptual knowledge, you will practice concrete validation steps. You'll learn to verify gRPC status and subscription state on IOS XE using commands that show whether the device is connected to the collector and the last-sent time. You will interpret what Disconnected, Connecting, and Active states mean in practice and how to proceed — for instance, checking the collector's firewall and service availability. You'll also learn how to reason about resource impact: streaming at sub-second intervals improves visibility but increases C P U and bandwidth usage, and you'll be able to explain tradeoffs and monitoring strategies. Finally, you'll become familiar with common troubleshooting checks: validating YANG XPath filters, ensuring collector redundancy, and confirming that buffer limits are handled or mitigated. These practical skills turn understanding into operational competence: you can both configure and verify a telemetry pipeline and decide when a push model is the right fit.

Start by defining the problem: traditional SNMP is pull-based. A network management system periodically queries devices for counter values or state. That approach works for coarse, infrequent monitoring, but it creates observable gaps. If you poll every five minutes, a one-second performance spike can occur and disappear between polls, leaving no trace. Polling also scales poorly: trying to poll many devices every second creates enormous overhead and increases latency. Streaming telemetry addresses this by letting devices push data either on change or at high frequencies, so you capture transient events and reduce the need for constant polling requests. A concrete example: collecting interface counters every second from hundreds of devices via polling would flood the NMS and consume C P U on both ends. With streaming telemetry, devices send updates only when configured or when a change occurs, lowering management-plane overhead and improving timeliness. A common misconception is that push always means more bandwidth; while higher-frequency streaming does increase data volume, well-designed subscriptions and YANG filters let you limit what you stream. The practical takeaway: choose streaming when you need sub-second visibility and use filters to control load.

Let's define streaming telemetry precisely. Streaming telemetry is a model where devices push structured operational data to a collector either when values change or at a configured frequency. It differs from logs and polling because data is delivered proactively and typically in a structured, schema-driven format. The advantage is immediate availability: collectors see changes soon after they occur, enabling faster anomaly detection and closed-loop automation. Concretely, you can stream interface statistics at one-second intervals so analytics detect link flaps or microbursts that would be invisible to coarse polling. A useful mental model is that telemetry turns devices into observability publishers and the collector into a subscriber that ingests time-series updates. A common misconception is that streaming always produces massive volumes; the reality is that using YANG filters and sensible update policies (on-change, periodic with tuned intervals) lets you control volume while still gaining timely data. The takeaway is clear: streaming telemetry trades configuration complexity for timeliness and granularity, and when combined with YANG it becomes machine-friendly for automation. What is Streaming Telemetry? means devices push structured operational data on change or periodically; yang filters and update policies control the volume and content.. In practical terms, a push-based, event-driven approach to operational data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

YANG is central to model-driven telemetry. It defines the shape and semantics of configuration and operational state so both devices and collectors agree on what each field means. In practice, YANG modules describe configuration nodes like interface IP addresses and operational nodes like interface statistics or C P U utilization. They can also define RPC operations and notification formats. When you specify a YANG XPath filter in a telemetry subscription, you're asking the device to stream a particular subtree defined by the model. A concrete example: the path /interfaces-state/interface/statistics points to per-interface counters described in the YANG module for interfaces. A common misconception is that YANG is a transport; it is not. YANG only defines structure and semantics; NETCONF or gRPC carry the data. Because YANG is vendor-neutral, collectors can parse telemetry from different devices consistently, simplifying automation and analytics. The practical skill is reading a YANG path and matching it to the telemetry you need, which reduces trial-and-error and avoids empty subscriptions. YANG Data Models: the schema for telemetry means yang defines what telemetry contains; transports move it. use yang paths to precisely specify telemetry data.. In practical terms, how yang defines configuration, operational state, rpcs, and notifications. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Understanding transports is about tradeoffs. NETCONF is an IETF protocol that uses XML encoding and typically runs over SSH. It is transaction-aware and well-suited to configuration tasks with strong operational semantics. NETCONF can also be used to retrieve state and subscribe to notifications, but XML encoding and SSH add overhead compared to binary transports. gRPC, by contrast, uses Protocol Buffers for serialization and HTTP/2 for transport; it supports streaming patterns, including bidirectional streams, and is generally more efficient on the wire. For streaming telemetry, gRPC's efficiency and native support for streaming make it attractive on IOS XE, especially when high-frequency updates are required. A common misconception is that NETCONF is obsolete; it remains useful for configuration transactions and for environments where XML and SSH are preferred. In practice, choose NETCONF for configuration and RPCs when you need transactional guarantees, and choose gRPC/Protobuf for high-performance telemetry streaming. Both depend on YANG models for the data structure; the transport only affects encoding and session behavior. NETCONF and gRPC: how data gets moved means netconf is xml-over-ssh and transaction-focused; grpc with protobuf is binary, http/2-based, and optimized for streaming high-frequency telemetry.. In practical terms, xml-over-ssh transaction model vs protobuf/http2 streaming. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Now we walk through the IOS XE configuration needed to enable gRPC so the device can act as a gRPC client or server depending on your model. Start in global configuration mode and enable the grpc service by specifying a port and ensuring the service is not shutdown. This step allows the device to establish or accept gRPC connections for telemetry. A concrete IOS snippet shows enabling gRPC on port 57000 and issuing no shutdown. After enabling gRPC you should verify the service state. A common trap is choosing a port already in use or forgetting firewall rules on the collector. Also confirm whether your deployment will use TLS; production setups should secure gRPC with TLS, whereas lab setups may use insecure channels for simplicity. The practical command and a quick verification step will prepare you to create subscriptions next. Remember: enabling gRPC is necessary but not sufficient — you still need to create telemetry subscriptions and ensure the collector is reachable. Enable gRPC on Cisco IOS XE means turn on the grpc service in global configuration, choose a port like 57000, and prepare for subscription configuration and collector connectivity checks.. This lesson walks through creating a telemetry subscription on IOS XE. A subscription defines what to stream, how to encode it, the update policy, and the receiver details. Start by creating a named subscription. Choose an encoding such as the Key-Value Google Protocol Buffer encoding indicated by encode-kvgpb, set a YANG XPath filter to target the data subtree you need, select the stream mechanism like cisco-push, define update frequency using update-policy periodic with a millisecond interval, and finally provide the receiver's IP, port, and protocol. A concrete example: a subscription named MY_SUBSCRIPTION that encodes with encode-kvgpb, filters /interfaces-state/interface/statistics, uses stream cisco-push, updates every 1000 milliseconds, and points to a collector at 192.168.1.40:57000 via grpc-tcp. Common mistakes include typos in the XPath filter and forgetting that the receiver must be reachable and listening as a gRPC server. After you create the subscription, use show telemetry ietf subscription to confirm state and last-sent-time. Deploying telemetry isn't only about commands; it's about avoiding common pitfalls. A frequent error is an incorrect YANG path: a small typo in an XPath filter leads to an empty stream. Always validate your YANG model and test filters with show telemetry commands. Network issues are another common blocker: firewalls often block gRPC ports like 57000, so verify connectivity using tcpdump or firewall logs. Collector availability matters; routers will buffer data up to a limit and then drop it if the collector is unreachable, so architect collector redundancy for critical metrics. Resource consumption is also a safety concern: highly granular streams increase C P U and bandwidth usage on devices — balance your need for granularity with device capabilities. Security must not be ignored: production deployments should use TLS and authentication for gRPC to prevent unauthorized access to telemetry. The practical habit is to start with conservative update policies and test one device before scaling, validate YANG paths, and build monitoring around collector health. Keep three ideas in mind. First, streaming telemetry is push-based and delivers near real-time, high-granularity data, which is essential to capture transient events that polling misses. Second, YANG models are the schema backbone: they define configuration and operational state, letting collectors parse telemetry consistently and avoiding vendor-specific ambiguity. Third, transports matter: NETCONF uses XML over SSH and suits transactional configuration tasks, while gRPC with Protocol Buffers and HTTP/2 provides an efficient, streaming-capable transport commonly used in high-frequency telemetry deployments on IOS XE. Together these elements allow a reliable, scalable telemetry pipeline when you validate YANG paths, secure gRPC connections, and verify collector reachability.
